questions.question: Between the 2023-2025 WMP and the 2026-2028 WMP, how did our risk ranking and grid hardening mitigation prioritization framework evolve? How did it impact how mitigations were selected and prioritized for circuit segments? (e.g. overall utility risk, risk per mile, benefit cost ratio, etc.)
questions.golden_answer: The governing concepts did not begin in 2026. The 2023-2025 Technical Guidelines already required a prioritization list based on Overall Utility Risk, geographic granularity down to circuit/segment/span/asset, multiple locally relevant alternatives for each risk driver, and comparison of expected risk reduction, cost, uncertainty, and schedule. SDG&E's 2023-2025 WMP implemented this through increasingly granular WiNGS-Planning versions, moved from partial locations toward full circuit-segment hardening, and used Risk Spend Efficiency (RSE) and risk reduction to inform covered-conductor and undergrounding choices. The 2026-2028 WMP makes that framework more explicit and auditable. WiNGS-Planning v4.0 reports Wildfire Risk, Outage Program Risk, and Overall Utility Risk by feeder segment; it provides both total-Overall-Utility-Risk rankings and a separate Overall Utility Risk-per-mile ranking; and it renames the selection metric Cost-Benefit Ratio (CBR), formerly RSE. CBR measures monetized risk reduction per unit of lifecycle cost and compares Strategic Undergrounding with Combined Covered Conductor while considering residual wildfire and PSPS risk. The result is a three-stage decision: risk scores identify high-risk segments; CBR and lifecycle/residual-risk analysis inform the mitigation type; then engineering feasibility, funding, permitting, schedule, resource efficiency, and constructability determine sequence. Therefore, the highest total-risk or highest risk-per-mile segment is not automatically built first, and the highest-ranked activity is not automatically selected. Adjacent segments may be bundled, inherited scopes from older WiNGS versions may remain, and lower-ranked work may proceed when it improves circuit-wide risk reduction or construction efficiency. Overall Utility Risk, risk per mile, and CBR answer different questions and should not be collapsed into one ranking.

questions.question: How would you evaluate our risk reduction strategy given the operational and grid hardening mitigations we have planned and established targets for across both WMP cycles? At a high-level this would be an exercise to quantify anticipated risk reduction across the various mitigations. (we have the waterfall chart in 26-28 WMP but it may not be as clear or straightforward in 23-25 WMP).
questions.golden_answer: The strategy is directionally coherent: sustained grid hardening reduces structural wildfire and PSPS risk, while operational measures manage residual risk before long-lead construction is complete. The 2026-2028 WMP's Figure 1-1 reports a common 2007 baseline of 100% wildfire risk, followed by 51.0% reduction attributed to system hardening, inspection, and vegetation management through 2025; another 2.5% from those activities during 2026-2028; 6.1% from SRP/FCP/EFD through 2028; 38.2% from PSPS plus situational awareness in 2028; and 2.2% unmitigated risk in 2028. These values sum to 100%, but they are not a clean comparison of the 2023-2025 and 2026-2028 WMP cycles: the 51.0% block covers 2007-2025, SRP/FCP/EFD spans 2012-2028, and PSPS/situational awareness is a 2028 residual-risk layer. The 2023-2025 plan reports annual initiative-level expected risk impacts and circuit-level planned mitigation, but the available evidence does not provide a single, reconciled 2023-2025 waterfall on the same basis. Therefore a defensible cross-cycle total cannot be calculated by adding plan target percentages or comparing the 51.0% and 2.5% blocks as if they represented equal three-year windows. A sound evaluation would use one frozen baseline and model version, avoid double-counting overlapping activities, separate wildfire from PSPS/PEDS effects, distinguish activity effectiveness from portfolio risk reduction, and report planned versus realized reduction at service-territory, activity, and circuit-segment levels. On the available evidence, the portfolio logic is strong, but cross-cycle numerical comparability remains incomplete.

questions.question: Comparing the 2023-2025 WMP, 2026-2028 WMP, and corresponding guidelines, what are opportunities for improvement in how we explain our risk methodology and assessment as well as our mitigation selection and prioritization?
questions.golden_answer: The largest opportunity is not to add more terminology, but to make the chain from inputs to construction sequence reproducible. First, publish a concise crosswalk for each cycle from guideline requirement to WMP section, table, model output, and owner. Second, explain model inputs, assumptions, limitations, uncertainty propagation, validation, version changes, and any use of conservative or maximum consequence values; distinguish Overall Utility Risk, Wildfire Risk, Outage Program Risk, total risk, risk per mile, activity effectiveness, expected portfolio risk reduction, and CBR/RSE. Third, for each prioritized area show at least two locally feasible mitigations with risk-driver effects, pre/post risk, lifecycle cost, CBR/RSE, uncertainty, schedule, and residual risk. Fourth, separate the three decisions: which locations rank highest, which mitigation is selected, and when it is constructed. Document every qualitative override, engineering constraint, funding limitation, bundling decision, and subject-matter judgment that changes the quantitative rank order. Fifth, show wildfire-versus-PSPS/PEDS trade-offs and the time value of risk during long construction lead times, including interim mitigations. Sixth, reconcile every narrative commitment with the applicable target table and QDR tracking ID. These improvements directly join requirements already present in the 2023-2025 guidelines with OEIS's findings on maximum-consequence aggregation, PSPS trade-off transparency, undergrounding alternatives and time value of risk, third-party model recommendations, and omitted measurable targets. The 2026-2028 WMP provides substantially more explicit CBR, risk-per-mile, activity-effectiveness, and circuit-level risk tables, but it should still disclose data/model lineage and explain why actual selection or sequencing differs from any displayed ranking.

questions.question:
What WMP unit targets did SDG&E repeatedly not meet during the 2023-2025 WMP cycle? (2023-2025 SDG&E’s AIR and the independent evaluator report are references for this, as well as the OEIS report for SDG&E’s 2023 performance)
4.1 What are the primary reasons those unit targets were not met?
4.2 Were they within SDG&E’s control or due to external factors (i.e. easements, permitting, etc.)?
questions.golden_answer: The cited AIR and independent-evaluator reports are not in the corpus, so this is a Table 1 proxy rather than a regulatory finding. Defining 'repeatedly' conservatively as a Q4 reported actual below the annual quantitative target in all three years, four tracking IDs qualify: WMP.463 Advanced Protection/System Automation (4 of 5 circuits in 2023, 5 of 8 in 2024, 7 of 8 in 2025); WMP.488 Distribution Overhead Patrol Inspections (85,857 of 86,880 structures; 86,140 of 86,197; 86,040 of 86,535); WMP.549 Distribution Communications Reliability Improvements/System Automation (11 of 35 base stations; 3 of 60; 4 of 5); and WMP.555 Transmission 69kV Tier 3 Visual Inspections (1,602 of 1,632 structures; 1,605 of 1,632; 1,601 of 1,632). The source explicitly marks WMP.463 and WMP.549 delayed. WMP.463 reasons changed by year: a circuit was held because substantial undergrounding was planned, crews were reallocated to undergrounding and covered conductor, and permits were not issued until January 2026. WMP.549 cites engineering-design delay during telecom-team onboarding, a program revision following the 2024 GRC, and a field change order after unknown subsurface facilities were discovered. These are mixed-control causes: staffing, onboarding, sequencing, and resource allocation are substantially internal; GRC funding, permit issuance, and unknown field conditions are external or shared. WMP.488 and WMP.555 are marked Complete/Completed despite small numeric shortfalls, and Table 1 gives no corrective-action reason; it is unsafe to infer a cause or call them compliance failures without the AIR/evaluator methodology. Other activities missed in two years, but this answer uses the stricter all-three-years definition to avoid an arbitrary threshold.

questions.question: Compare the WMP to the WMP guidelines. Flag any areas that need additional information to meet the guideline requirements.
questions.golden_answer: The question does not identify a WMP cycle, and the corpus contains both 2023-2025 and 2026-2028 plans and guidelines. A formal line-by-line compliance determination therefore requires a cycle-specific crosswalk. For the 2023-2025 cycle, the strongest evidence-backed gaps are those confirmed by OEIS: insufficient explanation of maximum-consequence aggregation and future probability-distribution work; inadequate transparency into wildfire-versus-PSPS trade-offs and how risk rank/risk buy-down affected selection; insufficient comparison and justification of undergrounding alternatives, including time value of risk; incomplete reporting of third-party model recommendations and disposition; and measurable situational-awareness commitments described in narrative but omitted from the target table. These map directly to guideline requirements for model assumptions/limitations/validation, multiple alternatives per risk driver with risk reduction/cost/uncertainty/schedule, transparent prioritization, circuit-level pre/post risk, and auditable target tables. For 2026-2028, the WMP supplies substantially more of this information through Overall Utility Risk and risk-per-mile tables, CBR comparisons, activity-effectiveness and expected-risk-reduction tables, circuit-level annual risk, schedules, constraints, and interim mitigations. Remaining items to flag for review include fields explicitly reported as n/a (especially outage-program effectiveness or CBR for many activities), assumptions based on subject-matter judgment or limited historical data, the reconciliation of changing baselines/model versions with target risk reduction, and exact explanations whenever construction order differs from displayed risk rank. This is a prioritized gap assessment, not certification that every guideline row is satisfied.

questions.question: Review the WMP from OEIS’s perspective and provide suggestions for how to present or and adjust the plan to satisfy what OEIS and the WMP guidelines are looking for. This could be done for past cycles to develop the AI agent, but would be help for evaluating the 2028-2031 WMP as we develop it.
questions.golden_answer: A formal compliance finding on the 2028-2031 WMP is not possible because a 2028-2031 draft is not present in the corpus. Based on OEIS's decision on SDG&E's 2023-2025 WMP and the 2026-2028 WMP Guidelines, SDG&E should make the next plan auditable from risk inputs through location-level project selection and measurable results. First, document the risk calculations, assumptions, uncertainties, validation, and model governance. In particular, address OEIS's concern that aggregating maximum consequence values can overstate territory risk: transition to probability distributions or validate and explain any alternative, and disclose which third-party model recommendations are adopted, rejected, and scheduled. Second, make mitigation selection reproducible. For each prioritized circuit or segment, identify the local risk drivers, compare at least two feasible activity portfolios, and show expected reductions in overall utility, wildfire, and outage-program risk; implementation cost; RSE or CBR; uncertainty; schedule; constraints; and the reason for the selected portfolio. Explain any case where a lower risk-buy-down activity is selected over a higher-ranked one. Third, explicitly show wildfire-versus-PSPS trade-offs, the role of subject-matter judgment, and any overrides of quantitative rankings. Fourth, compare undergrounding with combinations such as covered conductor, inspections, vegetation management, and protective-device settings; incorporate deployment time, cumulative risk exposure, and interim mitigations into the comparison. Fifth, connect the portfolio to required tables: show pre- and post-mitigation overall utility risk for high-risk circuits, activities by implementation year, and consistent measurable targets. Every measurable commitment described in narrative text should also appear in the applicable target table. Finally, include an OEIS issue-closure matrix that maps each prior Area for Continued Improvement to the corrective action, owner, milestone, evidence, current status, and exact WMP location. These changes would directly address OEIS's prior concerns about risk-ranking transparency, justification of undergrounding, time value of risk, model improvements, and incomplete target tables while aligning the plan with the newer activity-selection and prioritization requirements.

questions.question: For example, "what numbers we have reported from 2022-2025 regarding detailed inspection and show the line chart, how does SDGE perform detailed inspection, at what frequency, are there any changes or enhancement after 2025 (this requires WMP 2026-2028)."
questions.golden_answer: For Distribution Overhead Detailed Inspections (WMP.478), the available Table 1 data begin in 2023; no authoritative 2022 inspection-count actual was found, so a 2022 point must be shown as unavailable rather than inferred. Reported year-end Q4 actuals were 11,755 structures in 2023, 16,503 in 2024, and 17,950 in 2025, against annual targets of 11,100, 15,450, and 13,275. SDG&E describes a thorough visual ground assessment of poles, attachments, conductors, cables, and relevant equipment; equipment may be opened, tested, or operated, and tools such as infrared, drones, binoculars, or measurement devices may be used when warranted. Findings are recorded in work orders, repairs are assigned severity under GO 95 Rule 18, and corrective work is tracked. GO 165 sets a five-year cycle for overhead structures and sub-equipment, including the HFTD. After 2025, the 2026-2028 WMP states that no change was made to program scope or frequency and lists no planned program improvements. It does describe operational responses: drones/helicopters for difficult terrain, a six-month Qualified Line Inspector training program to relieve labor pressure, and planned engagement with the CPUC on whether GO 165 could permit more proactive risk-informed timing. Targets rise to 21,924 inspections in 2026, then decline to 17,779 in 2027 and 11,537 in 2028, totaling 51,240; those are targets, not actuals and should not be joined to the historical actual line as observed performance.
